objectives: Place modern, postmodern, jazz, hip-hop + tap on a stylistic map.
Survey major global folk + classical forms — flamenco, Bharatanatyam, Kathak.

slides.title: Ballet — classical, neoclassical, contemporary
slides.body:
Ballet is one tradition with three internal genres separated by a century each.

**Classical ballet** is the Petipa-era Imperial Russian heritage (1862-1910, St Petersburg Mariinsky). **Marius Petipa** (1818-1910) defined the classical pas de deux structure (entrée + adagio + variations + coda), the **grand divertissement** (long suite of short character + virtuoso variations), the **corps de ballet** as architectural element, the use of mime + character dance inside a story. Key works: *La Bayadère* (1877), *The Sleeping Beauty* (1890), *The Nutcracker* (1892), *Swan Lake* (1895 with Lev Ivanov), *Raymonda* (1898). Music by Tchaikovsky, Minkus, Glazunov. Pointe + turnout + symmetry + virtuosity-inside-structure. Most major companies (Mariinsky, Bolshoi, Royal Ballet, Paris Opera, ABT) still pivot their repertory around the Petipa works.

**Neoclassical ballet** is the **George Balanchine** revolution (1928-1983, NYCB). Balanchine retained classical vocabulary + technique but stripped:
- Narrative — many works plotless (*Serenade* 1934, *Agon* 1957, *Symphony in Three Movements* 1972).
- Mime — gesture absorbed into pure movement.
- Heavy production — practice clothes, bare stage, single light.
- Symmetry — off-balance attacks, asymmetric formations.
What remained + intensified: pure music visualization. Balanchine's dictum 'See the music; hear the dance.' Faster tempi, sharper attack, sustained extension, eccentric musicality. Trained in Russia, formed by Diaghilev, settled in America 1933 + co-founded SAB (1934) + NYCB (1948). Trained generations of American ballerinas — Tallchief, Farrell, Verdy, Kistler.

**Contemporary ballet** is the post-Balanchine wave: **William Forsythe** (b.1949, Frankfurt + Forsythe Company); **Jiří Kylián** (b.1947, Nederlands Dans Theater); **Mats Ek** (b.1945); **Wayne McGregor** (b.1970, The Royal Ballet); **Crystal Pite** (b.1970, Kidd Pivot). Vocabulary still grounded in pointe + turnout + adagio + allegro but extended with:
- Floor work, release, contact improvisation, contemporary-dance influences.
- Spoken text (Pite + Jonathon Young's *Betroffenheit* 2015 + *Revisor* 2019).
- Cinematic mass formations + ensemble counterpoint (Pite, McGregor).
- Algorithmic deconstruction of ballet grammar (Forsythe's Improvisation Technologies; P89 L2).
- Mocap + AI process (McGregor + Random International; P89 L8).

Each generation builds on, rather than discards, the previous; ballet is the most archaeologically deep dance tradition.

slides.title: Modern, postmodern + Tanztheater
slides.body:
**Modern dance** (1900-1960, primarily American + German). Founders Isadora Duncan + Ruth St Denis + Loie Fuller (P89 L1) rejected ballet; **Martha Graham** (1894-1991), **Doris Humphrey** + Charles Weidman, **José Limón**, **Hanya Holm** (German lineage from Mary Wigman + Laban) codified American modern from 1926. **Lester Horton** (LA) + **Katherine Dunham** (Afro-Caribbean influence) added the West-Coast + Black branches. **Pearl Primus** + **Alvin Ailey** carried Black-American modern into the canon (Ailey's *Revelations* 1960 remains the most-performed modern work in the world).

From the 1950s, **Merce Cunningham** + **Paul Taylor** + **Erick Hawkins** broke off in distinct directions — Cunningham toward chance + abstraction (P89 L1); Taylor toward muscular Americana; Hawkins toward Asian-influenced spatial work.

**Postmodern dance** (1962-mid-1980s). Centered on the **Judson Dance Theater** at Judson Memorial Church, NYC, 1962-1964. **Yvonne Rainer**'s *No Manifesto* (1965) is the canonical text: 'No to spectacle. No to virtuosity. No to transformations + magic + make-believe. No to the glamour + transcendency of the star image. No to the heroic. No to the anti-heroic. No to trash imagery. No to involvement of performer or spectator. No to style. No to camp. No to seduction of spectator by the wiles of the performer. No to eccentricity. No to moving or being moved.' The Judson refusals open the field to pedestrian movement, task scores, walking, standing, sitting.

Key Judson + post-Judson figures: **Trisha Brown** (1936-2017, *Accumulation* 1971, *Set and Reset* 1983 with Robert Rauschenberg + Laurie Anderson, the Equipment Pieces walking on walls + roofs), **Steve Paxton** (1939-2024, invented contact improvisation 1972 with *Magnesium*), **Lucinda Childs**, **David Gordon**, **Deborah Hay**, **Simone Forti**.

**Contact improvisation** (Paxton 1972) — weight-sharing between two bodies through a rolling point of contact — becomes a global movement form taught everywhere by the 1980s + a foundation of contemporary training (P89 L2).

**Tanztheater** (Germany, 1970s+). **Pina Bausch** (1940-2009) at Tanztheater Wuppertal from 1973 fuses dance + theatre + autobiography + scenography. Repetition + ensemble + emotionally exposed performance (P89 L1). **Reinhild Hoffmann, Susanne Linke, Johann Kresnik** are the parallel German Tanztheater generation.

**Late-modern + crossover**. **Bill T. Jones** (b.1952), Black queer political modern + contemporary (*Last Supper at Uncle Tom's Cabin* 1990, *Still/Here* 1994); **Garth Fagan** (Jamaican-American, *The Lion King* 1997 choreography); **Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker** (Belgium, Rosas, *Fase* 1982); **Ohad Naharin** (Israel, Batsheva, Gaga technique); **Akram Khan** (UK, Kathak + contemporary).

slides.title: Jazz + hip-hop + tap + global folk + classical forms
slides.body:
**Jazz dance** is Broadway + film + concert hybrid with African-American vernacular roots (cakewalk, Charleston, Lindy Hop, Black Bottom). Twentieth-century concert + theatrical jazz codified by:
- **Jack Cole** (1911-1974), 'father of theatrical jazz', fused Indian + Afro-Caribbean + ballet vocabularies.
- **Matt Mattox** (1921-2013), jazz-class syllabus that became the dominant West Coast school.
- **Bob Fosse** (1927-1987), the most recognisable American jazz style — turned-in feet, isolated shoulders, finger snaps, derby hats, sliding sideways. Choreographed *Chicago* (stage 1975, film 2002), *Cabaret* (film 1972), *Sweet Charity* (1966), *Pippin* (1972), *All That Jazz* (1979). Multiple Tony + Oscar + Emmy wins.
- **Eugene Louis 'Luigi' Faccuito** (Luigi technique).
- **Gus Giordano** (Chicago jazz).
- **Frank Hatchett** (commercial jazz, NYC Broadway Dance Center).

**Hip-hop dance**. Family of Black + Latino vernacular forms born in NYC + LA from late 1960s (P89 L2 for full vocabulary). Key originators:
- **Don 'Campbellock' Campbell** (LA, 1969), inventor of **locking** + leader of the Lockers.
- **Sam 'Boogaloo Sam' Solomon** + **Skeeter Rabbit** (Fresno + LA, 1970s), founders of the **Electric Boogaloos** + the **popping** family.
- **DJ Kool Herc** + the Bronx block parties (1973+) → **b-boying / breaking**.
- **Crazy Legs** (Richard Colón, b.1966) of the **Rock Steady Crew** — the most influential b-boy of the late 1970s + 1980s; embodied breaking's spread to film (*Wild Style* 1983, *Beat Street* 1984, *Flashdance* 1983) + then to global culture.
- **Tommy the Clown + Tight Eyez** (LA, 2000s) for **krumping** (*Rize* 2005 documentary by David LaChapelle).
- **Buddha Stretch, Henry Link, Brian Green** (NYC, 1990s) for the **hip-hop choreography** style on music videos + concerts.
Now Olympic discipline (b-boying / breaking added at Paris 2024 — P89 L8).

**Tap dance**. American + African-American vernacular percussion-on-feet. **Bill 'Bojangles' Robinson** (1878-1949) — vaudeville + Broadway + Shirley Temple films. **John Bubbles** (1902-1986) invented rhythm tap. **Honi Coles** (1911-1992), **Sandman Sims**, **Buster Brown**, **Jimmy Slyde** — the Hoofers' Club masters. **Gregory Hines** (1946-2003) carried tap into 1970s-90s film + television (*The Cotton Club* 1984). **Savion Glover** (b.1973) — protégé of Hines + Sims + Slyde — choreographed *Bring in 'da Noise, Bring in 'da Funk* (1996, Tony), *Happy Feet* (2006 motion capture for the penguins).

**Global folk + classical forms** are too many for one slide; three indispensable references:
- **Flamenco** (Andalusia). *Cante* (song), *toque* (guitar), *baile* (dance). *Cuadro* (group) + *zapateado* (rhythmic footwork). Major figures: Carmen Amaya, Antonio Gades, Joaquín Cortés, Sara Baras, Israel Galván (post-flamenco). Cycle structures: *soleá*, *bulería* (12-beat), *seguiriya*.
- **Bharatanatyam**. South Indian classical (Tamil Nadu), formalised from the *devadasi* temple tradition. Solo female lineage; structure: *alarippu* + *jatiswaram* + *shabdam* + *varnam* + *padam* + *javali* + *tillana*. *Mudras* (hand gestures), *adavus* (basic step units), *abhinaya* (facial + bodily expression). Tala counted in cycles (*tintal* 16 beats, *adi* 8 beats). Rukmini Devi Arundale + Balasaraswati codified mid-20C.
- **Kathak**. North Indian classical (Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras gharanas). Spins (*chakkar*), footwork (*tatkar*) with ankle bells (*ghungroo*), spoken rhythmic syllables (*bols*). Birju Maharaj (Lucknow gharana, 1938-2022) is the canonical 20C-21C figure. Akram Khan reworks Kathak into contemporary stage work.

Other crucial forms: **butoh** (Japan, 1959+ Hijikata + Ohno); **capoeira** (Brazil); **Argentine tango**; **Cuban son + rumba + salsa**; **kuchipudi, odissi, manipuri, mohiniyattam, kathakali** (other Indian classical forms); **Yoruba dance + sabar + adumu** (West + East African); **kabuki** (Japan); **Beijing opera**; **gumboot** (South Africa); **step + stepping** (African-American collegiate).

question.question: Locate five works on the genre map
question.goal: Given five works, name the genre + a defining signature for each.

acceptedAnswers: neoclassical ballet — Stravinsky 12-tone score + practice clothes + plotless

steps.reveal: Neoclassical ballet. Stravinsky 12-tone score, plotless, dancers in black-and-white practice clothes, single-light stage, classical vocabulary + off-balance attack. Defines Balanchine's NYCB style + the neoclassical genre.

acceptedAnswers: postmodern dance — pedestrian, anti-virtuosic, anti-spectacle (Judson lineage)

steps.reveal: Postmodern dance. *Trio A* (or *The Mind Is a Muscle, Part 1*, 1966) is the canonical Judson-era postmodern work: continuous unstressed movement, no eye contact with audience, no virtuosity, no climax. Embodies the 1965 *No Manifesto*.

Tanztheater (German dance-theatre). Music by Henry Purcell; sleepwalking figures; chairs scattered onstage; repetition + emotional exposure; fusion of dance with theatre + scenography + autobiography. The signature genre of Pina Bausch at Tanztheater Wuppertal.

acceptedAnswers: theatrical jazz — Fosse signature: turned-in feet + shoulder isolations + derby hats

steps.reveal: Theatrical jazz, Fosse style. Turned-in feet, sideways slide, isolated shoulders, finger snaps, derby hats. *Cabaret* (1972) won Fosse an Oscar; *Pippin* (1972) won a Tony; *Liza with a Z* (1972) an Emmy — the same year hat-trick.

steps.prompt: Work 5: Crazy Legs in *Wild Style* (1983) — b-boy battle.

acceptedAnswers: b-boying / breaking — Rock Steady Crew + Bronx origin + battle vocabulary

steps.reveal: B-boying / breaking. Crazy Legs (Richard Colón) of the Rock Steady Crew is the canonical late-1970s + 1980s b-boy figure; *Wild Style* (1983, Charlie Ahearn) brought breaking to global cinema. Toprock + downrock footwork + freezes + power moves (windmills, flares). Now an Olympic discipline (Paris 2024).

question.question: Which document is the canonical postmodern-dance manifesto?
options: Yvonne Rainer's *No Manifesto* (1965) — the canonical postmodern-dance manifesto. The full text is a sequence of refusals: 'No to spectacle. No to virtuosity. No to transformations + magic + make-believe. No to the glamour + transcendency of the star image. No to the heroic. No to the anti-heroic. No to trash imagery. No to involvement of performer or spectator. No to style. No to camp. No to seduction of spectator by the wiles of the performer. No to eccentricity. No to moving or being moved.' Written in the orbit of the Judson Dance Theater (1962-1964 at Judson Memorial Church, NYC). Defined the refusal-based postmodern aesthetic that runs through Brown, Paxton, Childs, Gordon, Hay + that still echoes in contemporary practice.
Doris Humphrey's *The Art of Making Dances* (1959).
question.explanation: Yvonne Rainer's *No Manifesto* (1965) is the canonical postmodern-dance text. Issued in the Judson Dance Theater orbit; a sequence of 'No to...' refusals (spectacle, virtuosity, glamour, heroic, style, seduction). Defined the postmodern aesthetic from Brown + Paxton + Childs forward.
question.workedSolution: Yvonne Rainer's *No Manifesto* (1965) is the canonical postmodern-dance text — a sequence of refusals: no to spectacle, virtuosity, transformations + magic, the star image, the heroic + anti-heroic, trash imagery, performer-spectator involvement, style, camp, seduction, eccentricity, being moved. Written in the Judson Dance Theater orbit (NYC 1962-1964) + defines the refusal-based postmodern aesthetic that flows through Trisha Brown, Steve Paxton, Lucinda Childs + others.

question.question: A genre-crossing programming decision
question.prompt: You curate a one-month international festival of 8 programmes. Programme constraints: 2 ballet, 2 modern/contemporary, 1 postmodern, 1 hip-hop, 1 tap, 1 global classical. Available companies: New York City Ballet (Balanchine triple bill), Forsythe Company, Alvin Ailey, Rosas (De Keersmaeker), Trisha Brown Company, Rock Steady Crew + Jonzi D, Dorrance Dance (Michelle Dorrance tap), Aakash Odedra Kathak. Build the 8-programme schedule + justify the through-line: what shared question or thread runs across the festival, how the genres talk to each other, where you put the most-conservative + most-experimental works in the schedule + how you brief the audience between programmes.

question.question: A flamenco *bulería* is in a 12-beat cycle with stresses on counts 3, 6, 8, 10, 12. How many stressed counts are there per cycle?

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, draw a stylistic map of dance from classical ballet to hip-hop, naming at least six choreographers / originators from at least four different genres. Note one global classical form + one diasporic vernacular form.
question.rubric: Should span: classical ballet (Petipa), neoclassical ballet (Balanchine), contemporary ballet (Forsythe + McGregor + Pite), American modern (Graham + Humphrey + Limón + Ailey), postmodern (Rainer + Brown + Paxton), Tanztheater (Bausch), theatrical jazz (Cole + Mattox + Fosse), tap (Robinson + Hines + Glover), hip-hop / funk styles (Don Campbell locking; Skeeter Rabbit popping; Crazy Legs breaking + Rock Steady Crew), global classical (Bharatanatyam, Kathak — Birju Maharaj, flamenco — Carmen Amaya or Israel Galván). Should articulate that each genre carries its own body politics + history (court / national / ethnic / urban) + that 21C choreographers regularly cross genre boundaries (Akram Khan crossing Kathak + contemporary; Hofesh Shechter crossing Israeli folk + contemporary; Camille A. Brown crossing African-American vernacular + concert dance).
